title: Reactive Oxygen & O2 Sensing
terms: Oxygen (O2) is essential for almost all life, but organic compounds are flammable, so O2 is also deadly and must be regulated.
Highly reactive, oxygen-containing compounds; their reactivity makes them very toxic.
Molecule with an unpaired electron; the most dangerous ROS are often free radicals.
The most basic ROS: single-electron reduction of molecular oxygen (O2 + 1 e− → O2−·). Other ROS form from it.
ROS formed spontaneously from superoxide; substrate for catalase, glutathione peroxidase, thioredoxin, and myeloperoxidase.
Highly reactive free-radical ROS; made by the Fenton reaction, ionizing radiation, and peroxynitrite breakdown.
Hydroperoxyl radical; listed among ROS (S6) and drawn as a Fenton reaction product (S10).
Nitrogen-containing reactive species made by nitric oxide synthase; nitrogen species can also be strong ROS.
Nitrogen radical; objectives call it the 'nitrite radical'. Forms when peroxynitrite breaks down.
Formed when nitric oxide radical reacts with superoxide; breaks down into ·NO2 and HO·.
To take electrons away. ROS are strong oxidizers that remove electrons from other atoms.
ROS change metal oxidation states: Fe2+ → Fe3+ and Cu+ → Cu2+.
Cysteine thiol (–S–H) oxidized to –SO2− then –SO3−, or two thiols joined into a disulfide (–S–S–).
Basel: "not super needing you to know" beyond it being on thioredoxin reductase; selenium = micronutrient for antioxidant defense (transcript).
One radical oxidizes something and makes a NEW radical, so one radical causes hundreds–thousands of damage events until two radicals meet (transcript).
First step: radical ROS takes an electron from R–H, making a new radical R·.
Each new radical steals an electron from another molecule, making another radical; repeats x times.
Two radicals combine (W· + N· → W–N), ending the chain.
Electron transport chain as ROS source
Complexes I and III always leak a little superoxide (coenzyme Q gives an electron to O2). Normal; also a signal that mitochondria are working (transcript).
Ischemia: succinate builds up; at reperfusion electrons run backward from Complex II into Complex I, leaking superoxide.
Accumulates at Complex II during ischemia (red arrow fumarate → succinate); drives backward electron flow to Complex I and superoxide on reperfusion.
Phagocytes "bleach/burn" bacteria: NADPH oxidase → superoxide → SOD → H2O2 → myeloperoxidase → HOCl (bleach); some leaks out (transcript).
Enzyme: NADPH + 2 O2 → NADP+ + H+ + 2 O2−·. Starts the respiratory burst; also an O2 sensor in glomus cells.
In basically every cell: superoxide → H2O2 ("still bad stuff") (S14, transcript).
Phagocyte enzyme: H2O2 + HCl → HOCl (bleach) + H2O.
'Bleach'; the killing product of myeloperoxidase in the phagosome.
Iron turns weak ROS (H2O2) into strong radicals (HOO·, HO·). Why free iron is never allowed: transferrin (blood) and ferritin (cell) hold it (transcript).
Enzyme: arginine + NADPH + H+ + O2 → citrulline + H2O + NADP+ + nitric oxide radical (·NO).
X-rays, gamma, high-energy electrons. Mostly hits WATER (far more water than DNA) → radicals + superoxide → oxidative stress (transcript).
Oxidized DNA, cross-linked DNA, DNA adducts.
Lipid peroxides and lipid adducts; multiplied by radical chain reactions.
Oxidized amino acids, protein dimers, protein adducts.
Cell damage → cell death, neoplasm, other diseases, and aging (slide puts '?' after aging).
Overdose overwhelms glucuronidation → oxidation route makes NAPQI → liver damage once glutathione runs out. Cats: no safe dose (transcript).
Main safe route: adds a sugar so acetaminophen can be excreted (bile/kidney). CATS LACK this enzyme (transcript).
Minor side pathway that produces NAPQI, a strong oxidizer.
Strong oxidant made from acetaminophen by cytochrome P450 oxidation; neutralized by glutathione until glutathione is depleted (transcript).
Treatment for acetaminophen toxicity: a glutathione building block the liver takes up (glutathione itself can't cross membranes). ~50/50 prognosis (transcript).
H2O2 → water + O2 ("safe stuff"). In bacteria, catalase can be a VIRULENCE FACTOR (resists the respiratory burst) (transcript).
Protein antioxidant with two close cysteines → S–S bond. Too expensive to be just an antioxidant; its real job is SIGNALING (hyperoxia/ASK1) (transcript).
Regenerates reduced thioredoxin using NADPH; contains selenocysteines. TrxR inhibitors are possible anti-cancer drugs.
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (reduced): electron donor that powers thioredoxin and glutathione regeneration cycles.
Glutamate–cysteine–glycine. "Easily the MOST IMPORTANT intracellular antioxidant"; cheap; regenerated with NADPH (transcript).
Oxidized glutathione: two GSH joined by a disulfide after reducing H2O2.
Enzyme: regenerates 2 GSH from GS–SG using NADPH; slide labels it 'selenocysteines!' (see flag).
Main EXTRACELLULAR (blood) antioxidant; relatively stable radical; regenerates vitamin E. Water soluble → megadoses are peed out. Deficiency = scurvy (transcript).
Fully oxidized vitamin C: 2 R· + 2 Asc → 2 R–H + Asc + DHAsc.
Lipid (MEMBRANE) antioxidant: aliphatic tail sits in membranes; regenerated by vitamin C (transcript).
Carries iron in the BLOOD so free iron can't drive Fenton reactions (transcript).
OUTSIDE — confirm: cell-surface receptor that takes up iron-loaded transferrin by endocytosis. Listed in terms, not shown.
Stores extra iron INSIDE the cell so it can't drive Fenton reactions (transcript).
Normal / low / high oxygen levels; each triggers different signaling responses.
Brainstem; sense CO2 (pCO2) only, not O2 (transcript).
Carotid and aortic bodies; respond to pO2 as well as pCO2 and pH; sense O2 through glomus cells.
Peripheral (carotid + aortic body). O2 keeps K+ channels open; low O2 → K+ closes → depolarize → voltage-gated Ca2+ in → SNARE → neurotransmitter. High O2 = low signaling (transcript).
Uses O2 to make carbon monoxide (CO), which keeps glomus K+ channels open in normoxia (transcript).
Low O2 → less ATP, more AMP → AMP kinase closes glomus K+ channels (transcript).
In glomus cells, makes superoxide from O2 during normoxia; superoxide signals to the K+ channel (keeps it open).
Transcription factors; in normal O2, prolyl hydroxylase oxidizes them → proteasome. Low O2 → survive → hypoxia-protective genes (transcript).
Uses O2 to add –OH to HIF in normoxia, targeting HIF for proteasomal degradation.
Fate of hydroxylated HIF when O2 is high.
Genes HIF turns on when O2 is low and HIF escapes degradation.

Apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1, a MAPKKK. Reduced thioredoxin inhibits it; hyperoxia oxidizes thioredoxin → ASK1 released → MAPK → hyperoxia genes (more glutathione) → apoptosis if severe. "Be able to trace out that pathway" (transcript).
Mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade: ASK1 (MAPKKK) activates MAPKK, then MAPK → pro-apoptotic gene expression.
Hyperoxia response output of the ASK1–MAPK pathway.
O2 has 2 unpaired electrons (triplet); organic molecules are singlet, so O2 'can't' react with you (forbidden transition) unless activated. Chemistry NOT required (transcript).
Hemoglobin with its iron oxidized (Fe2+ → Fe3+); cannot carry oxygen (transcript).
Liver oxidizing (redox) enzymes; turn excess acetaminophen into NAPQI (transcript).
Vitamin C deficiency: can't hydroxylate proline (hydroxyproline) properly (transcript).
traps: Reduction makes the oxidizer: superoxide is the single-electron reduction of O2 (O2 gains an e−), yet ROS act as oxidizers (take electrons away). Don't flip which word goes where (S6, S7).
Superoxide dismutase vs catalase: superoxide dismutase makes H2O2 + O2 (still bad stuff); catalase makes H2O + O2 (not bad stuff). Order: dismutase first, catalase second (S14).

Peroxidase vs reductase: glutathione peroxidase uses GSH to destroy H2O2 (GSH → GS–SG); glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH. Same logic for thioredoxin vs thioredoxin reductase (S15, S16).
Reduced vs oxidized thioredoxin: reduced (S–H H–S) = active antioxidant AND holds ASK1 off; oxidized (S–S) = releases ASK1 → apoptosis (S15, S25).
HIF flips with O2: high O2 → prolyl hydroxylase adds OH → degraded; low O2 → HIF survives → hypoxia response genes. Hydroxylation needs O2 (S24).
O2 sensing flips: glomus hypoxia closes K+, opens Ca2+, cell depolarizes (normoxia = polarized). Central receptors sense CO2 (as pH), NOT primarily O2; peripheral sense pO2 + pCO2 + pH (S22, S23).
Cat acetaminophen: cats lack glucuronidation (the major non-toxic route), NOT hydroxylation. Hydroxylation (minor) makes NAPQI. N-acetylcysteine is a GSH precursor, not an enzyme (S12, S19).
Respiratory burst order: NADPH oxidase → superoxide → superoxide dismutase → H2O2 → myeloperoxidase + HCl → HOCl. Myeloperoxidase acts on H2O2, not superoxide (S10).

Fenton = iron (header 'Fe2+'), inputs 2 H2O2, outputs HOO· + HO· (not superoxide in). NOS: arginine → citrulline + ·NO. Ischemia builds up succinate (not fumarate). Glutathione = glutamate (not glutamine)–cysteine–glycine (S9, S10, S16).
Selenocysteine placement (slide): thioredoxin reductase (S15) and glutathione reductase (S16) — not the peroxidase on these slides. Textbooks differ (see flag).

Vitamin C regenerates vitamin E (not the reverse). Slide: E radical "very stable", C "relatively stable"; transcript called both "relatively stable." C = blood (water), E = membranes (lipid), glutathione = inside the cell.
Toxicity timing: acetaminophen damage starts when glutathione is depleted, not when NAPQI first forms. Treat with N-acetylcysteine (glutathione itself can't cross membranes).
Catalase flip: protective for you, but a virulence factor when bacteria make it.
Hyperoxia vs hypoxia sensors: hypoxia → HIF survives · hyperoxia → oxidized thioredoxin releases ASK1 (reduced thioredoxin holds it).

Prolyl hydroxylase adds OH → proteasomal degradation

quiz.stem: Superoxide anion, the most basic reactive oxygen species, is formed by which process?
bad: Hydroxylation of molecular oxygen by iron
quiz.why: O2 + 1 e− → O2−·: gaining one electron is a single-electron reduction.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT a stage of a free radical chain reaction?
quiz.why: S8 lists initiation, propagation, termination. Dismutation is what superoxide dismutase does.

quiz.stem: During the propagation stage of a radical chain reaction, what happens?
quiz.ok: A radical takes one electron, creating a new radical
bad: Two radicals combine, forming one stable covalent bond
An enzyme converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide
A radical donates two electrons to molecular oxygen
quiz.why: Each radical steals one electron from another molecule, making a new radical; termination is radical + radical.

quiz.stem: In a neutrophil phagosome, NADPH oxidase has just produced superoxide. Which enzyme acts next in the respiratory burst?
bad: Nitric oxide synthase, producing peroxynitrite anion
quiz.why: Burst order: NADPH oxidase → superoxide dismutase (H2O2) → myeloperoxidase (HOCl).

quiz.stem: Myeloperoxidase produces bleach in the phagosome by combining hydrogen peroxide with which substrate?
bad: Arginine, forming citrulline and nitric oxide
quiz.why: H2O2 + HCl → HOCl + H2O (S10).

quiz.stem: In the Fenton reaction, which metal ion does the slide name as catalyzing hydroxyl radical formation from hydrogen peroxide?
quiz.why: S10 panel header: 'Fe2+ and the Fenton Reaction' (2 H2O2 → H2O + HOO· + HO·).

quiz.stem: Nitric oxide synthase uses NADPH and O2 to convert arginine into which products?
quiz.why: Arginine → citrulline + ·NO (S10).

quiz.stem: A dog has a femoral artery clot removed after hours of limb ischemia. Which metabolite built up during ischemia and drives a superoxide burst at reperfusion?
quiz.why: S9: succinate builds up at Complex II during ischemia; reperfusion → superoxide.

quiz.stem: A cat given Tylenol after a fall presents cyanotic, drooling, and lethargic. Why is acetaminophen so toxic in cats?
quiz.ok: Cats lack glucuronidation, so the dose goes to NAPQI
bad: Cats lack hydroxylation, so the dose goes to NAPQI
Cats lack catalase, so hydrogen peroxide accumulates
Cats lack glutathione, so NAPQI cannot be formed
quiz.why: Glucuronidation is the main non-toxic route; without it, all of the dose goes to NAPQI.

quiz.stem: The same acetaminophen-toxic cat needs treatment. Which choice matches the slide's treatment and its rationale?
quiz.ok: N-acetylcysteine, to restore reduced glutathione stores
bad: Vitamin E, to regenerate oxidized vitamin C stores
Superoxide dismutase, to neutralize NAPQI directly
N-acetylcysteine, to block hydroxylation of acetaminophen
quiz.why: NAPQI is detoxified by GSH; N-acetylcysteine is a GSH precursor.

quiz.stem: Which enzyme uses NADPH to convert glutathione disulfide (GS–SG) back into two reduced glutathione molecules?
quiz.why: Peroxidase consumes GSH on H2O2; reductase regenerates GSH with NADPH.

quiz.stem: Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of which three amino acids?
quiz.why: S16: glutamate–cysteine–glycine.

quiz.stem: After vitamin E quenches a lipid radical, it becomes a stable radical itself. Which antioxidant regenerates it?
quiz.why: S18 shows vitamin C donating H+ + e− to the vitamin E radical.

quiz.stem: Which statement about the central respiratory receptors is correct?
quiz.ok: They sense mainly CO2 as pH, not oxygen
bad: They sense mainly oxygen through glomus cells
They sit in the carotid and aortic bodies
They sense pO2, pCO2, and pH equally
quiz.why: Central (ventrolateral medulla) receptors do not primarily sense O2.

quiz.stem: A carotid body glomus cell becomes hypoxic and its K+ channels close. What happens next?
quiz.why: K+ closed → depolarize → Ca2+ channels open → neurotransmitter release.

quiz.stem: In a well-oxygenated cell, what happens to hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)?
quiz.ok: Prolyl hydroxylase adds OH, targeting HIF for degradation
bad: Prolyl hydroxylase adds OH, activating hypoxia response genes
AMP kinase phosphorylates HIF, targeting it for degradation
Thioredoxin reduces HIF, releasing it into the nucleus
quiz.why: High O2 → hydroxylated HIF → proteasome; low O2 → HIF survives.

quiz.stem: During hyperoxia, how does the ASK1 pathway become activated?
quiz.ok: Oxidized thioredoxin releases ASK1, activating MAPKK then MAPK
bad: Reduced thioredoxin releases ASK1, activating MAPKK then MAPK
Oxidized thioredoxin binds ASK1, blocking MAPKK and MAPK
Thioredoxin reductase phosphorylates ASK1, activating MAPK directly
quiz.why: Reduced Trx holds ASK1; H2O2 oxidizes Trx → ASK1 free → MAPK cascade → pro-apoptotic genes.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a product of ROS damage to macromolecules?
quiz.why: S11: oxidized/cross-linked DNA, DNA adducts; lipid peroxides/adducts; oxidized amino acids, protein dimers/adducts. Glucuronide is from the acetaminophen case, not ROS damage.

quiz.stem: A cat is given acetaminophen. Why is there no safe dose for cats?
quiz.ok: Cats lack glucuronidation, so all of it becomes NAPQI
bad: Cats lack cytochrome P450, so it accumulates unchanged
Cats lack catalase, so NAPQI is not broken down
Cats lack N-acetylcysteine, so glutathione can't form
quiz.why: Cats lack the glucuronidation enzyme; 100% goes through oxidation to NAPQI.

quiz.stem: In acetaminophen toxicity, when does severe liver damage begin?
quiz.ok: Once liver glutathione is depleted by NAPQI
bad: As soon as the first NAPQI is formed
Once vitamin C in the blood runs out
quiz.why: Glutathione neutralizes NAPQI first; damage starts when it runs out.

quiz.stem: Why is N-acetylcysteine given instead of glutathione for acetaminophen toxicity?
quiz.ok: Glutathione can't cross membranes; NAC is a building block
bad: NAC is a stronger oxidant that destroys NAPQI
NAC restores glucuronidation in the cat liver
Glutathione is toxic to hepatocytes at high doses
quiz.why: Liver takes up N-acetylcysteine and uses it to rebuild glutathione.

quiz.stem: Which antioxidant did Basel call the most important INTRACELLULAR antioxidant?
quiz.why: Glutathione: cheap tripeptide, abundant in every cell.

quiz.stem: Match each antioxidant to its main location: vitamin C, vitamin E, glutathione.
quiz.why: Vitamin C = water-soluble, extracellular; vitamin E = lipid tail in membranes; glutathione = intracellular.

quiz.stem: A bacterium survives inside neutrophil phagosomes. Which enzyme it makes best explains this?
quiz.ok: Catalase, breaking down the phagocyte's H2O2
bad: NADPH oxidase, making its own superoxide
quiz.why: Bacterial catalase is a virulence factor: it removes H2O2 from the respiratory burst.

quiz.stem: A cell is exposed to hyperoxia. Which sequence follows?
quiz.ok: Thioredoxin oxidized → ASK1 released → MAPK → apoptosis
bad: Thioredoxin reduced → ASK1 bound → MAPK → survival
HIF hydroxylated → ASK1 released → MAPK → apoptosis
Thioredoxin oxidized → HIF released → MAPK → apoptosis
quiz.why: Reduced thioredoxin holds ASK1 (a MAPKKK); oxidation releases it → MAPK → hyperoxia genes, then apoptosis.

quiz.stem: Why does taking megadoses of vitamin C not build up antioxidant protection?
quiz.ok: It is water soluble, so excess is excreted in urine
bad: It is lipid soluble, so excess is stored in fat
It is converted to vitamin E, which is then excreted
It inhibits glutathione synthesis at high doses
quiz.why: Water-soluble: more in, more peed out.

quiz.stem: Why must free iron be bound by transferrin and ferritin?
quiz.ok: Free iron drives Fenton reactions, making strong radicals
bad: Free iron inhibits superoxide dismutase in all cells
Free iron binds glutathione and blocks regeneration
Free iron converts NAPQI back into acetaminophen
quiz.why: Fenton: iron turns H2O2 into HOO· and HO· radicals.

quiz.stem: Ionizing radiation enters a cell. What is it most likely to hit first, and what results?
quiz.why: Cells have far more water than DNA; radiolysis makes ROS.

flags: 'LC20!' cross-reference (S7, S9)

Slides point to 'LC20' for electron transport / oxidation-state content. In Bethany's Exam 3 notes the electron transport/ischemia lecture was LC17 (OUTSIDE — confirm 2026 numbering) · review that Exam 3 lecture for Complex I–IV details.
'Nitrite radical' (S4) vs ·NO2 (S6)

S4 objectives say 'nitrite radical'; S6 figure shows ·NO2 (nitrogen dioxide radical; nitrite is NO2−) · treat as the same item; use 'nitrogen dioxide radical (·NO2)' and recognize 'nitrite radical' on the exam.
Slide typos

'glucurorinidation' and 'Acetominophen' (S12), 'fumurate' (S9), 'Citruline' (S10), 'antixodiants' (S13), 'Stuart, Ira, and Fox' (S21; one author, Stuart Ira Fox) · correct spellings: glucuronidation, acetaminophen, fumarate, citrulline, antioxidants.
'Hydroxylation' naming (S12)
Slide calls the NAPQI route 'hydroxylation'. OUTSIDE — confirm: textbooks describe cytochrome P450 oxidation · use the slide's word.
Ischemia/reperfusion mechanism (S9) — checked

Checked against slide image: red arrows show succinate build-up at Complex II (fumarate → succinate) and electrons driven backward from Complex II quinol into Complex I, leaking superoxide; red X's on proton pumping and Complex IV O2. Superoxide also drawn at Complex III. This matches the textbook reverse-electron-transport model · know it from the figure; confirm wording with transcript.
Central receptors 'increased pH' (S22)

Checked against slide image: S22 really reads 'in response to increased pH (and increased pCO2)'. Rising pCO2 lowers pH (raises H+) · genuine slide error; use 'increased pCO2 / increased H+ (decreased pH)' and confirm with transcript.
NADPH stoichiometry (S15, S16)
Net equations show H2O2 + 2 NADPH + H+ → 2 H2O + 2 NADP+. OUTSIDE — confirm: one H2O2 needs 2 electrons = 1 NADPH · don't memorize coefficients; know NADPH powers regeneration.
HIF details (S24)

Slide gives only prolyl hydroxylase → proteasome vs hypoxia response genes. OUTSIDE — confirm: HIF-1α, von Hippel–Lindau protein, erythropoietin/vascular endothelial growth factor targets · not responsible unless transcript adds them.
TrxR inhibitors 'WHY?' (S25)

Stop-and-think with no answer on slide. Inferred answer (OUTSIDE — confirm): blocking thioredoxin reductase leaves thioredoxin oxidized → ASK1 released → MAPK → pro-apoptotic genes in cancer cells · confirm with transcript.
'aging (?)' (S11)
Slide itself questions ROS → aging · treat as possible, not established.
S10 equations — checked

Checked against slide image: Fenton = iron (header 'Fe2+', ball labeled Fe^x+) + 2 H2O2 → H2O + HOO· + HO· (no superoxide input). NOS = 2 arginine + 3 NADPH + 3 H+ + 4 O2 → 2 citrulline + 4 H2O + 3 NADP+ + 3 ·NO. The NOS figure doesn't balance (2 arginine → 3 ·NO) · don't memorize coefficients; know arginine → citrulline + ·NO.
Selenocysteine location — CLOSED by transcript
Basel tied selenium to thioredoxin reductase (matches slide); not needed beyond that · use the slide.
Transferrin/ferritin — CLOSED by transcript
Transferrin carries iron in blood; ferritin stores it in cells; both block Fenton chemistry.
Glomus CO — CLOSED by transcript
Heme oxygenase makes CO, which keeps K+ channels open in normoxia; superoxide also keeps them open; AMP kinase closes them in hypoxia. Basel: 'I don't care that much about systems.'
Feline acetaminophen — mostly closed
Transcript: liver damage from NAPQI after glutathione depletion; also mentions hemoglobin damage. Use liver/glutathione framing.
Vitamin E radical stability
Slide S18: 'very stable'; transcript: 'relatively stable' · if asked, E is the more stable of the two per slide; don't overthink.
Last slide (TrxR inhibitors)
Basel skipped it: 'Don't worry about this.'
